title: How to Tell a Great Story
author: Athenaeum Book Club
summary: This Athenaeum Book Club essay, written as an accompaniment to the group's reading of Moby-Dick, asks why Melville stretches the novel form almost to breaking point. It argues that the book's strange features are deliberate characterization of the narrator rather than digressions. Because the story is a first-person account, everything from the opening line "Call me Ishmael" to the etymology of the word "whale" and the extract collection reflects Ishmael's psychology. The scholarly chapters, such as the "Cetology" chapter, show a man who cannot stop gathering information about whales. The essay concludes that Ishmael is a traumatized narrator whose obsession is his way of processing what he witnessed, and that the experimental structure is therefore part of the theme. It is a short example of reading a canonical novel by asking what kind of writer would include each feature, and it ends with an invitation to join the club's readings.
points: Moby-Dick's first-person frame means its oddities are evidence about the narrator, so readers should treat structure as characterization.
The opening etymology and extracts show Ishmael compiling information obsessively without making it a coherent narrative.
Asking "what kind of writer puts this in his story?" is a productive reading habit for any difficult canonical work.
The scholarly cetology chapters are read as symptoms of Ishmael's trauma and obsession, not as irrelevant detours.
The essay reframes the novel's genre-bending experimentation as the way it conveys its themes of obsession and fate.
quotes: Every storyteller knows the story he wants to tell. But how to tell that story to be the story his listeners want to hear is much more difficult. And how to make sure that the two are the same thing is the hardest of all.
This establishes something important about the novel: it’s not an unbiased reporting of the story. It’s a first-person account, deliberately set up as a relating of the story to the reader.

Ishmael is collecting every piece of information he can find and compiling it into this book, with neither interest nor attempt at making it form a coherent or helpful narrative. He’s dumping whatever information he can find about whales into his book.
In fact, the question “what kind of writer puts this in his story?” is exactly the kind of question you should be asking. We know that Ishmael wrote this tome.

The events of the story he is telling have affected him deeply; the book even seems to show that he has been genuinely traumatized, and that the writing of this story is Ishmael’s attempt to process that trauma.
If you read Moby-Dick on your own, it can be tempting to skip right to Chapter 1 and its famous line, “Call me Ishmael.” But that’s not actually how the novel begins.
Moby-Dick is the record of a man who has lost his own identity in an obsession that springs from his own traumatic experience.
